steps.description: Create a Python script that implements the bootstrap rigidity probe using small feedforward networks. The script will: (1) generate a family of abstract constraints (e.g., polynomial interpolation or functional inequalities), (2) sweep constraint sample counts w, (3) for each w, find the minimal hidden layer width N_c(w) that achieves zero violation on held-out points, (4) record N_c(w) vs w trend and train/holdout violation metrics. Files to modify: none (new script). Prediction: The script will run without errors and produce a table of N_c(w) values; if the underlying constraint set is rigid, N_c(w) will plateau or decrease as w increases; if the solution space is fat, N_c(w) will increase with w. SKILL: None (custom ML experiment). FILES: rigidity_probe.py

plans.objective: [DIM: topology] The rigidity transition in the solution space is governed by the Betti number of the constraint manifold: as w increases, β₀(w) should drop from >1 to 1 at a critical threshold, indicating a shift from disconnected solution components to a single rigid set.

steps.description: The hypothesis concerns the relationship between constraint count (w) and the minimum network capacity (N_c(w)) required to achieve zero violations in a bootstrap solution space. I will design and execute a numerical experiment using a small feedforward neural network to probe this rigidity transition. The experiment will systematically vary the number of constraints (w) and measure the minimum hidden layer width (N_c) that achieves zero violation on held-out constraints. This will determine whether the solution space becomes more rigid (N_c decreases/stays constant) or fatter (N_c increases) as constraints are added. I'll implement the experiment in Python, run the grid search, and analyze the N_c(w) trend to validate or refute the hypothesis.
